title: Park your work, deal with the emergency, come back
summary: A production bug arrives while you are halfway through a feature. Stash the mess, fix the bug, restore the mess — and learn why untracked files need an extra flag.
mental_model: A stash is a commit that is not on any branch. `push` makes it and cleans your tree; `pop` applies it and deletes it; `apply` applies it and keeps it. That is the whole model.

write.content:
def ramp(start, end):
    pass  # not done yet

steps.title: The interruption arrives
steps.why: One modified file, one brand-new file, neither finished. You cannot commit this and you cannot switch branches carrying it. This is what stash is for.

steps.title: Stash — and notice what stays behind
steps.why: By default stash takes tracked modifications only. ramp.py is untracked, so it is left sitting in your working tree, which is rarely what you meant.
steps.expect: pump.py is clean again; ramp.py is still there as ??.

steps.title: Do it properly with -u
steps.why: `-u` includes untracked files. Now the tree is genuinely clean and the whole piece of work is in one stash entry — which is what you want before switching branches.
steps.expect: Working tree completely clean, one stash entry.

verify.label: the tree is clean, untracked file included
one stash entry holds the work

steps.title: Fix the bug on a clean tree
steps.why: This is the payoff: the emergency fix is made against exactly what is committed, with none of your half-finished work leaking into it.

steps.title: Bring the work back
steps.why: `pop` applies the stash and removes it from the list. Both the modification and the untracked file return, exactly as you left them.
steps.expect: Your half-finished work is back, and the stash list is empty.

verify.label: and so did the untracked file

steps.title: apply, when you want to keep the entry
steps.why: `apply` leaves the stash in the list — useful when applying the same work to two branches, or when you are not yet sure the restore worked. `drop` removes it when you are.
steps.expect: After apply the entry is still listed; after drop it is gone.

steps.title: See that a stash is just commits
steps.why: `stash list` is a reflog of the `stash` ref, and each entry is a real commit object with your work in its tree. Nothing exotic — which is why the recovery tricks for commits work on stashes too.

verify.label: the work is restored to the working tree
your half-finished modification survived the round trip
verify.hint: git stash push -u, then git stash pop

verify.label: the untracked file survived too — that is what -u buys you
the emergency fix was committed on a clean tree

pitfalls: Without `-u`, untracked files stay behind and end up in the wrong commit on the wrong branch. Make `-u` your default.
`git stash` with no message gives you 'WIP on main: abc1234'. After three of those you cannot tell them apart — always use `-m`.
Stashes are not pushed and not shared. A stash you leave for a week is a stash you will not remember.
`pop` on a conflict leaves the entry in the list, deliberately, so you cannot lose it while resolving.
cheatsheet: restore the newest and remove it
